question: It is 14 September 2026. A program office needs urgent repair parts and field service support to return a grounded fleet to service and wants a $48 million not-to-exceed undefinitized contract action issued tomorrow. The PM asks you to obligate $36 million now 'before the money expires on 30 September.' The contractor says it will send a proposal 'in a couple of months.' What can you do, and on what terms?
answer:
A UCA may be the right tool, but not on those terms.

When and who. DoD uses a UCA only when a definitive contract cannot be negotiated in time and performance must begin immediately (DFARS 217.7403). The HCA approves a request explaining why work must start now and what delay would cost (217.7404-1; PGI 217.7404-1). Army Appendix GG (Rev. 30) lets the HCA delegate approval no lower than the chief of the contracting office below $50 million, and the SCO above, so I confirm our delegation. A letter contract also needs the HCA's written determination that no other contract is suitable (RFO FAR 16.603-3).

Terms:
- A $48 million not-to-exceed price (217.7404-2).
- Definitization by the earlier of 180 days after a qualifying proposal or the date obligations exceed 50 percent of the NTE (217.7404-3(a); 10 U.S.C. 3372(a)(1)).
- A proposal due date; if the qualifying proposal is late, I can withhold up to 5 percent of later financing requests (217.7404-3(b)).

The money. Before a qualifying proposal I may obligate no more than 50 percent of the NTE, $24 million. The limit rises to 75 percent, $36 million, only if the proposal arrives before 50 percent is obligated, and I obligate only what the undefinitized period requires (217.7404-4; 10 U.S.C. 3372(a)(2)). Expiring funds are no exception, and a fiscal-year deadline is not a waiver basis (217.7404-5). So the answer to the PM is $24 million at most.

Follow-through: progress payments capped at 80 percent (32.501-1(d)); a preliminary subcontracting plan now (19.206-3(f)); profit that reflects the reduced cost risk (217.7404-6); and the semiannual UCA report, since it exceeds $5 million (217.7405).

Cite: DFARS 217.7403, 217.7404-1 through 217.7404-6, 217.7405 and PGI 217.7404-1 (Class Deviation 2026-O0027); RFO FAR 16.603-3, 19.206-3(f), 32.501-1(d); AFARS 5117.7404-1 and Appendix GG; 10 U.S.C. 3372 and 3374.
key_points: UCAs only when a definitive action cannot be negotiated in time and performance must start now; HCA approval (DFARS 217.7403, 217.7404-1); Army delegation per Appendix GG Rev. 30 (no lower than CoCO below $50M, no lower than SCO above $50M).
Definitize by the earlier of 180 days after a qualifying proposal or obligations exceeding 50% of NTE; extension beyond an additional 90 days needs HCA determination (217.7404-3(a)).
Obligate no more than 50% of NTE before definitization, up to 75% only after a qualifying proposal, and only what the undefinitized period needs (217.7404-4).
Late qualifying proposal: withhold up to 5% of subsequent financing requests (217.7404-3(b)); profit reflects reduced cost risk (217.7404-6).

80% progress payment cap on UCAs (32.501-1(d)); UCAs over $5M reported semiannually (217.7405); a UCA over $50M cannot be unilaterally definitized without written approval, a copy to the contractor and a 30-day wait (10 U.S.C. 3372(b) names the service acquisition executive; DFARS 217.7404(b) names the HCA without redelegation).

mcq.stem: A DoD UCA has a $48 million not-to-exceed price. The contractor submitted a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the NTE was obligated. What is the most that may be obligated before definitization?

options.text: 75 percent of the NTE, $36 million, and only as much as the undefinitized period requires
options.why: DFARS 217.7404-4(a) and 10 U.S.C. 3372(a)(2)(B) raise the limit to 75 percent after a timely qualifying proposal; 217.7404-4(b) limits obligations to actual needs.

options.text: 50 percent of the NTE, $24 million, regardless of the proposal
options.why: 50 percent is the limit before a qualifying proposal; a timely qualifying proposal allows up to 75 percent.

options.text: 80 percent of the NTE, the progress payment limit for undefinitized actions
options.why: 80 percent (32.501-1(d)) caps progress payments on undefinitized work; it is not the obligation limit.

options.text: 100 percent, if the funds expire at the end of the fiscal year
options.why: There is no fiscal-year-end exception to the obligation limits; waivers are for specific operational needs such as contingency, humanitarian or peacekeeping operations (217.7404-5(b)).

question: You awarded a $31 million dining facility services contract on Wednesday, 2 September 2026. You debriefed the incumbent on 8 September, it submitted written follow-up questions on 10 September, and you delivered written answers on 15 September. On Friday, 18 September, GAO notifies you that the incumbent has protested. The incumbent's contract ends 30 September. The garrison commander tells you to let the new contractor start on 1 October and says he will sign whatever paperwork is needed. What do you do?
answer:
First, the stay applies. For DoD, if GAO's notice arrives within the latest of 10 days after award, 5 days after an offered debriefing date, or 5 days after a postaward debriefing concludes, I must immediately suspend performance or terminate (DFARS 233.105-70, in lieu of RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(1)). A DoD debriefing concludes when we deliver written answers to timely follow-up questions (DFARS 215.301-71(c)). Our answers went out 15 September; day five is Sunday the 20th, so the window runs through Monday, 21 September (4 CFR 21.0(d)), and the 18 September notice is inside it. I tell the awardee in writing not to start and seek a no-cost suspension (33.105-3(d)).

Second, neither the commander nor I can override. Only the HCA, nondelegably, may authorize performance, on a written finding that it is in the best interests of the United States or that urgent and compelling circumstances will not permit waiting for GAO, and only after GAO is notified (33.105-3(b)(2), (c); 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(3)(C), (e)). I send the HCA's findings to ODASA(P) (AFARS 5133.105-3(b)).

Third, I give the HCA an honest package: the mission impact of a feeding gap, alternatives such as a short incumbent extension or an urgency bridge (6.103-2), their costs, and counsel's view of the protest. GAO must decide within 100 days (31 U.S.C. 3554(a)(1)), so a bridge need only cover that. An override can be challenged at the Court of Federal Claims, and a thin finding invites a second fight.

Meanwhile I notify counsel and start the agency report, due 30 days after GAO's notice (33.105-4(a); 31 U.S.C. 3553(b)(2)(A)).

Cite: RFO FAR 33.105-3, 33.105-4(a), 6.103-2; DFARS 233.105-70 (Class Deviation 2026-O0026 Rev. 1), 215.301-71 (2026-O0048 Rev. 1); AFARS 5133.105-3(b); 31 U.S.C. 3553, 3554(a); 4 CFR 21.0(d).
key_points: DoD stay windows: latest of 10 days after award, 5 days after an offered debriefing date, or 5 days after the debriefing concludes (DFARS 233.105-70); a DoD debriefing concludes when written answers to follow-up questions are delivered (215.301-71(c)); a period ending on a weekend or holiday runs to the next business day (4 CFR 21.0(d)).

Postaward override: HCA only, nondelegable, written finding of best interests of the U.S. or urgent and compelling circumstances, GAO notified first (RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(2)-(c); 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(3)(C), (e)).
Army: KO sends the HCA's written findings to ODASA(P) as soon as practicable (AFARS 5133.105-3(b)).
Weigh alternatives such as a bridge or urgency justification; GAO decides within 100 days (31 U.S.C. 3554(a)(1)); overrides can be challenged at the Court of Federal Claims.
Preaward override is urgent and compelling only, with award likely within 30 days (33.105-2(b)); agency report due 30 days after notice.

mcq.stem: After a timely GAO protest of a DoD contract award, who may authorize the awardee to continue performance, and on what basis?

options.text: The HCA, nondelegably, on a written best-interests or urgent-and-compelling finding, after notifying GAO
options.why: RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(2)-(c) and 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(3)(C) and (e) set the official, both bases and the notice requirement.

options.text: The garrison commander, as head of the requiring activity, on a written finding of mission necessity
options.why: Only the head of the contracting activity may authorize performance, and the authority cannot be delegated.

options.text: The contracting officer, once the agency report has been filed with GAO and legal counsel concurs in writing
options.why: The KO has no override authority; filing the agency report or getting counsel's concurrence does not lift the stay.

options.text: The HCA, on a best-interests finding, both before and after award
options.why: Best interests is available only after award; a preaward override requires urgent and compelling circumstances and award likely within 30 days (33.105-2(b)).

question: On 1 September 2026 you received a $4.3 million claim for differing site conditions on a construction contract. The certification is signed by the contractor's project manager and leaves out the statement that the amount requested accurately reflects the contract adjustment for which the contractor believes the Government is liable. Your supervisor says the claim is defective, so you can take as long as you like. What is your clock, and what do you do?
answer:
The clock is running, and ignoring it is how the Government loses control of a claim.

A claim over $100,000 must be certified in the language of 52.233-1(d) (RFO FAR 33.205-2(a); 41 U.S.C. 7103(b)). A certificate that alters or omits that language, or is signed by someone without authority to bind the contractor, is defective; no certification at all is not a defective certification (33.201). A defect does not defeat a board's or court's jurisdiction, and it must be corrected before judgment (33.205-2(c)).

My clock:
- Within 60 days of receipt, by 31 October, I either decide or tell the contractor when I will, and I decide within a reasonable time (33.205-6(c)(2), (d)).
- With a defective certification, I am relieved of the duty to decide only if, within those 60 days, I tell the contractor in writing why the certification is defective (33.205-6(e)). I send that letter now and log the receipt date (33.205-1(a)(2)).
- Silence past the deadline is a deemed denial the contractor can appeal (33.205-6(g)), and interest runs from 1 September even after the certificate is fixed (33.205-3(c)).

Working the claim: counsel and technical staff, DCAA audit support, the contractor's claims history (PGI 233.205-5), and ADR, which is often faster and cheaper (33.205-8). The contractor keeps performing (33.205-7). I settle only within my warrant (33.205-5(a)), and signs of fraud go to the fraud official, not a settlement (33.205-4).

The final decision gives my rationale and the appeal rights: 90 days to the ASBCA or 12 months to the Court of Federal Claims. I send it by a method that proves receipt and pay any amount found due without waiting for an appeal (33.205-6(a)-(b), (h)).

Cite: RFO FAR 33.201, 33.205-1 through 33.205-8; FAR 52.233-1(d); DFARS PGI 233.205-5 (Class Deviation 2026-O0026 Rev. 1); 41 U.S.C. 7103 and 7104.
key_points: Claims over $100,000 must be certified (RFO FAR 33.205-2(a); 41 U.S.C. 7103(b)); altered or missing language, or an unauthorized signer, is a defective certification; no certification at all is not (33.201).
Certified claims over $100K: decide within 60 days or notify the contractor of the decision date, and decide within a reasonable time (33.205-6(c)(2), (d)).
No duty to decide a claim with a defective certification only if the KO notifies the contractor in writing of the defects within 60 days (33.205-6(e)).
Missing the deadline is a deemed denial; interest runs from original receipt even after the certification is corrected (33.205-6(g); 33.205-3(c)).
Final decision includes rationale and appeal rights (90 days ASBCA, 12 months COFC), sent with proof of receipt; pay amounts found due without awaiting appeal (33.205-6(a)-(b), (h)).

options.text: Notifying the contractor in writing, within 60 days of receiving the claim, of the reasons the certification is defective
options.why: 33.205-6(e) removes the obligation to decide only when that written notice goes out within 60 days.

options.text: Nothing needs to be done, because a defective certification means no claim exists and no clock starts
options.why: A defective certification is not the same as no certification: jurisdiction survives (33.205-2(c)), interest runs from receipt (33.205-3(c)), and the 60-day notice is required.

options.why: 33.211 is the pre-RFO number, and the 60-day period runs from receipt of the claim, not from an audit.

question: In 2024 your office awarded a $52 million, five-year firm-fixed-price (noncommercial) training support services contract. On 1 August 2026 you issued a partial termination for convenience deleting two of the six sites. The contractor's settlement proposal asks for $3.1 million: $1.2 million in severance and unexpired lease costs, $900,000 in 'lost profit' on the four remaining years at the two sites, $400,000 in accounting and legal costs to prepare the settlement, and $600,000 in unamortized start-up and recruiting costs. How do you settle it?
answer:
Part 49 governs this noncommercial settlement; a commercial one would follow 12.304.

- The TCO negotiates and settles by determination only if we cannot agree (RFO FAR 49.103). The final proposal is due within one year of termination (49.206-1(a)).
- A settlement is a modification. Certified cost or pricing data are required when the partial settlement plus the estimate to complete the continued work exceeds the threshold (15.403-3(b)(3)(ii)(B)): $2.5 million for this DoD contract awarded before 1 July 2026 (DFARS 215.403-3(a)(1)). A proposal at or above the threshold must be audited (49.107(a)), and AFARS PGI 5149.107(a) sends every settlement proposal to the audit office within five calendar days.

- Lost profit on unperformed work: disallowed. Profit covers only work done and preparations, never settlement expenses or consequential damages (49.202(a)).
- Settlement preparation costs: generally allowable when reasonably necessary, but no profit (31.205-42(g)).
- Unexpired leases: rental less residual value, if the lease was reasonably necessary and the contractor tried to end or reduce it (31.205-42(e)).
- Start-up and recruiting costs: allowable initial costs if segregated and not also in overhead (31.205-42(c)).
- Severance: allowable only if required by law, agreement, established policy or the circumstances of the employment (31.205-6(f)).
- A contract headed for a loss gets no profit and a loss adjustment (49.203); excluding settlement costs, the total is capped at the contract price less payments (49.207).
- Any equitable adjustment for the remaining sites is separate, with no double counting (49.208).

Approvals. The settlement negotiation memorandum follows the PGI 249.110 format (49.110), agency review thresholds are local (49.111), and the agreement goes on an SF 30 (49.109-1).

Cite: RFO FAR 49.103, 49.107, 49.109-1, 49.110, 49.111, 49.202, 49.203, 49.206-1, 49.207, 49.208; 31.205-6(f), 31.205-42; 15.403-3(b)(3)(ii); 12.304; DFARS 215.403-3(a) (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev. 1); PGI 249.110 (2026-O0010); AFARS PGI 5149.107(a).
key_points: Noncommercial fixed-price terminations follow Part 49; commercial terminations follow 12.304 and 52.212-4 instead.

Settlements are modifications: certified data are required when the partial settlement plus the estimate to complete exceeds the threshold ($2.5M for DoD primes awarded on or before 30 Jun 2026), and proposals at or above it go to audit (15.403-3(b)(3)(ii); DFARS 215.403-3(a); 49.107(a)); AFARS PGI 5149.107(a) sends Army settlement proposals to the audit office within 5 calendar days.
No profit on unperformed work, settlement expenses or consequential damages (49.202(a)); loss adjustment if the contract would have lost money (49.203).

Termination cost principle 31.205-42: settlement expenses, unexpired leases, initial costs and unavoidable continuing costs are generally allowable under its conditions; severance only as 31.205-6(f) allows.
Total, excluding settlement costs, capped at contract price less payments (49.207); SNM per PGI 249.110; agency review under 49.111 with locally set thresholds.

question: You are about to solicit a $14.6 million firm-fixed-price barracks renovation at an Army installation in the United States. What bid guarantee, performance and payment bond, and liquidated damages requirements apply, and how do you set the liquidated damages rate?
answer:
Bonds. The Bonds statute (formerly the Miller Act) requires performance and payment bonds on construction over $150,000 (RFO FAR 28.102-1(a); 40 U.S.C. 3131).
- Performance bond: 100 percent of the original contract price, plus 100 percent of any increase, unless I determine a lesser amount is adequate (28.102-2(b)(1)).
- Payment bond: 100 percent unless I find in writing that is impractical, and never less than the performance bond (28.102-2(b)(2)).
- Bonds arrive before the notice to proceed (28.102-1(c)); clause 52.228-15 (28.102-3(a)).

Bid guarantee. Required whenever those bonds are (28.101-1(a)): at least 20 percent of the bid price, capped at $3 million, so $2.92 million here (28.101-2; provision 52.228-1). Construction takes only separate guarantees (28.101-1(b)). The chief of the contracting office may waive it for a specific acquisition such as overseas work (28.101-1(c)), which does not fit here. In sealed bidding a noncompliant guarantee means rejection unless an exception applies (28.101-4).

Liquidated damages. I evaluate the need in acquisition planning (36.101-5) and use them only when late completion will damage the Government in ways hard to estimate or prove (11.401(a)). They compensate, not punish (11.401(b)). The construction rate is per day of delay and includes daily inspection and superintendence plus other delay costs such as substitute property or quarters allowances (11.402(b)); clause 52.211-12 (11.403(b)). If the customer wants a big number 'so the contractor feels it,' I push back: an unsupported rate is a penalty that invites higher prices and disputes. Waiving assessed damages takes the head of the agency or designee plus Treasury approval (11.401(d)).

Also: an independent Government estimate before proposals (36.101-6), CPARS at $900,000 or more (42.1102(e)), and a warrant of at least $25 million.

Cite: RFO FAR 28.101-1, 28.101-2, 28.101-4, 28.102-1, 28.102-2, 28.102-3; 11.401 through 11.403; 36.101-5, 36.101-6; 42.1102(e); FAR 52.228-1, 52.228-15, 52.211-12; 40 U.S.C. 3131.
key_points: Construction over $150,000: performance and payment bonds at 100% of original contract price (plus increases) unless a lesser amount is justified; payment bond never below the performance bond (RFO FAR 28.102-1, 28.102-2).
Bid guarantee whenever bonds are required: at least 20% of the bid price, capped at $3 million; separate guarantees only for construction (28.101-1, 28.101-2(b)).
Bond waiver for work in a foreign country if impracticable (28.102-1(a)(1)); CoCO bid guarantee waiver only when not in the Government's interest (28.101-1(c)).

Liquidated damages only when delay harms the Government and damages are hard to prove; rate is a reasonable forecast, not a penalty; construction rate per day includes inspection and superintendence (11.401-11.402).
Clauses 52.228-15, 52.228-1, 52.211-12; IGE before proposals (36.101-6); CPARS for construction at $900K or more (42.1102(e)).

question: A garrison DPW wants an $18 million, five-year architect-engineer IDIQ contract for facility design work. The resource manager suggests getting price proposals from every interested firm and awarding to the lowest price with acceptable qualifications. How must A-E services be selected under the Brooks Act, and what limits apply?
answer:
Price shopping is what the Brooks Act prohibits.

The rule. A-E services are bought by qualifications-based selection, a competitive procedure (RFO FAR 36.102-2(a)-(b); 40 U.S.C. chapter 11).
- The requirement is publicly announced (36.102-1).
- An evaluation board reviews qualifications, holds discussions with at least three firms and ranks at least three most highly qualified firms (36.202-1; 40 U.S.C. 1103). Price is not a ranking factor.
- The selection authority makes the final ranking, cannot add firms and explains in writing if its top firm differs from the board's (36.202-2).
- I negotiate with the top firm; if we cannot reach a fair and reasonable price, I formally end negotiations and move to the next (36.202-3; 40 U.S.C. 1104).

Limits:
- For the Army, the fee for designs, plans, drawings and specifications cannot exceed 10 percent of estimated construction cost (10 U.S.C. 7540(b); DFARS 236.202-371, replacing the FAR's 6 percent at 15.404-9(c)(4)(ii)). My PNM signature documents the check (15.404-9(c)(4)(iv)).
- No award to a firm whose principals or associates sit on our evaluation board (36.202-3(e)).
- CPARS for A-E contracts of $45,000 or more (42.1102(f)).

Army specifics. Only USACE, the National Guard Bureau, MICC and ACC's 414th CSB (O&M and Army Family Housing projects) may contract for A-E services; others place task orders under USACE contracts by agreement (AFARS 5136.002-90). Selection authority is delegated through Appendix GG (AFARS 5136.202-2), so I first confirm our office's authority and selection official.

What I tell the resource manager: we control cost through the independent estimate (36.102-3), hard negotiation and the fee limit, not by making price a selection factor.

question: You have just reached price agreement on a $27 million sole-source contract priced with certified cost or pricing data. What must your price negotiation memorandum contain, and what Army approvals come before and after the negotiation?
answer:
Before I negotiate. Prenegotiation objectives come from my proposal analysis; with cost analysis they document the issues, cost objectives and profit objective (RFO FAR 15.408-1). With certified data, DoD requires a structured profit approach, normally weighted guidelines on the DD Form 1547 (DFARS 215.404-970). The Army requires written approval of the objectives before negotiating and allows a consolidated POM/PNM (AFARS 5115.408-190).

At agreement the contractor certifies its data accurate, complete and current as of price agreement (15.403-4).

The PNM records (15.408-2(a)):
- The purpose, the acquisition and the negotiators on both sides.
- Contractor system status as it affected the negotiation.
- Reliance on the certified data, and any defective data and its price effect.
- The proposal, field pricing and audit recommendations with reasons for variances, my objective and the result, by major cost element.
- The key facts behind the objective and the agreement, and significant differences.
- The quantified effect of outside direction.
- The profit objective and profit negotiated, and the fair and reasonable determination.

If I reject significant audit advice, I explain why (15.407(a)); a copy goes to the field pricing office (15.408-2(b)); and a contractor insisting on an unreasonable price goes above my level (15.407(d)).

After negotiation. If the price lands within the approved range and nothing undercuts it, the objectives approval can also approve a consolidated POM/PNM, but every other preaward approval still applies (AFARS 5115.408-290). Because this noncompetitive action exceeds $25 million, both documents go into CBAR within 30 days after award (PGI 215.408-2). Local business clearance thresholds still apply. The PNM is the Government's record in any later defective pricing case.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.403-4, 15.407, 15.408-1, 15.408-2; DFARS 215.404-970, 215.408-1, 215.408-2 and PGI 215.408-2 (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev. 1); AFARS 5115.408-190, 5115.408-290.
key_points: Army KOs must obtain written approval of prenegotiation objectives before negotiating any pricing action; the POM and PNM may be consolidated (AFARS 5115.408-190).

Prenegotiation objectives based on cost analysis document the issues, cost objectives and profit objective (RFO FAR 15.408-1); DoD uses a structured profit approach when certified data are obtained (DFARS 215.404-970(a)).

PNM contents (15.408-2(a)): participants, contractor system status, reliance on certified data and any defects, proposal vs. objective vs. negotiated result by major cost element, significant differences, outside direction, profit basis, fair and reasonable documentation.
Explain rejected audit recommendations (15.407(a)); the KO's signature documents compliance with statutory fee limits (15.404-9(c)(4)(iv)).

A consolidated POM/PNM approval can cover a final price within the approved range, but other preaward approvals and local business clearance thresholds still apply (AFARS 5115.408-290); DoD noncompetitive actions over $25M go into CBAR within 30 days after award (PGI 215.408-2).

question: You are placing a $9.5 million task order under an Army multiple-award IDIQ. What does fair opportunity require at that value, and what changes if the requiring activity wants the order placed sole source with one awardee?
answer:
Fair opportunity. Every awardee gets a fair opportunity for each order above the micro-purchase threshold unless a sole-source order is justified (RFO FAR 16.507-2(a)(1)). Part 6 and subpart 15.3 do not apply, so no competitive range or evaluation plan is required (16.507-2(a)(3)), but I may not allocate orders, and price or cost is always a factor (16.507-2(c)(1)).

Above $7.5 million (16.507-5; 10 U.S.C. 3406(d)):
- Fair notice to all awardees with clear requirements, a reasonable response period, and the significant factors, including price, and their relative importance.
- A record of fair consideration and, for best value, the weight of quality versus price.
- Postaward notices and debriefings under Part 15; DoD requires a debriefing for orders of $15 million or more (DFARS 216.507-5(c)).

Sole source. The order must fit an exception: urgency, one capable awardee, a logical follow-on, a minimum guarantee, a statute, or for DoD a 6.103 exception (16.507-6(b)). I write a Justification for an Exception to Fair Opportunity with the 16.507-6(d)(2) content and certifications. DoD uses the DFARS 206.104-71 table instead of the FAR's (DFARS 216.507-6(e)), so at $9.5 million my certification approves it, subject to any higher local requirement. The notice and justification go on SAM.gov and our website within 14 days, or 30 for urgency, for at least 30 days (16.507-6(f)). Set-aside orders need no justification (16.507-6(c)).

Challenges. An order this size can be protested only as exceeding the contract's scope, period or maximum value; for DoD, other grounds require an order over $35 million and go only to GAO (16.508). Complaints go to the ombudsman (16.507-2(b)), so the notice and evaluation record are the real safeguard.

Cite: RFO FAR 16.507-2, 16.507-5, 16.507-6, 16.508; DFARS 216.507-5(c), 216.507-6(e) (Class Deviation 2026-O0045 Rev. 1); DFARS 206.104-71 (Class Deviation 2026-O0017 Rev. 2); 10 U.S.C. 3406(d), (f).
key_points: Fair opportunity for every order above the MPT unless a justified exception applies; no allocation; price or cost is always a factor; not subject to Part 6 or subpart 15.3 (RFO FAR 16.507-2).

Orders above $7.5M: fair notice with a clear requirement, reasonable response time, and significant factors with relative importance; documented fair consideration; Part 15 notices and debriefings (16.507-5; 10 U.S.C. 3406(d)).
DoD requires a postaward debriefing for orders of $15M or more (DFARS 216.507-5(c)).

Sole-source orders need an exception and written justification; DoD approval follows the DFARS 206.104 table, with KO certification at $10M or below (DFARS 216.507-6(e)); post within 14 days, or 30 days for urgency (16.507-6(f)).
DoD order protests are limited to scope/period/maximum-value challenges or orders over $35M at GAO; the ombudsman handles complaints (16.508; 16.507-2(b)).

question: You are awarding a $32 million O&M-funded firm-fixed-price facilities maintenance services contract at Camp Humphreys to a U.S. prime. The proposed workforce is 12 U.S. citizens hired in the United States, 300 Korean nationals hired locally, and 8 Philippine technicians hired in Manila. The apparent low offeror priced Defense Base Act insurance only for the 12 Americans, saying Korean workers 'aren't covered by DBA.' The requiring activity asks why DBA matters on a services contract at all. How do you answer, and what goes in the contract?
answer:
DBA matters, and the offeror is only partly right.

Why it applies. The Defense Base Act covers employees outside the continental United States on U.S. public-work contracts, including service contracts connected with national defense (42 U.S.C. 1651(a)(4), (b)(1); RFO FAR 28.305(a)-(b)). Base maintenance qualifies, whatever the employee's nationality, and DBA coverage carries War Hazards Compensation Act protection (28.305(c)).

Who can waive it. Not the contracting officer: the Secretary of Labor, on an agency head's recommendation (42 U.S.C. 1651(e); 28.305(d); DoD procedures at PGI 228.305(d)). In the Army that recommendation is delegated from ASA(ALT) to the HCA, no lower than the SCO (Appendix GG).

The Korea waiver. DoL Waiver No. 2026-02 (26 March 2026 to 25 March 2031) covers all contracts in Korea, but only employees covered by Korea's compulsory workers' compensation laws with a fully compliant employer. It excludes U.S. citizens, lawful U.S. residents and anyone hired in the United States. Third-country nationals' benefits must survive repatriation, and waived employees still need War Hazards Compensation Act-equivalent protection.

- 12 Americans hired stateside: DBA required.
- 300 Korean nationals: waived if covered by Korean compulsory law and the employer complies; otherwise DBA.
- 8 technicians hired in Manila: waived only if Korean compulsory law covers them with benefits that survive repatriation; otherwise DBA. I get the offeror's written position.
Correcting the offeror's DBA pricing is a proposal revision for negotiations, not a clarification (15.202(a)(2)(iii)).

Clauses. 52.228-3 where DBA applies and 52.228-4 where it is waived (28.309); with this mixed workforce I expect both, confirmed with policy and 411th CSB practice. For waived employees the contractor carries workers' compensation and war-hazard liability (28.305(e)).

Cite: 42 U.S.C. 1651(a)(4), (b)(1), (e); RFO FAR 28.305, 28.309, 15.202(a)(2); FAR 52.228-3, 52.228-4; DFARS PGI 228.305(d) (Class Deviation 2026-O0005); AFARS 5128.305(d), Appendix GG; DoL DBA Waiver No. 2026-02.
key_points: DBA covers contractor and subcontractor employees under U.S. contracts for public work outside the continental U.S.; public work includes service contracts connected with the national defense, regardless of employee nationality (42 U.S.C. 1651(a)(4), (b)(1); RFO FAR 28.305).

Only the Secretary of Labor can waive DBA, on an agency head's recommendation (42 U.S.C. 1651(e); 28.305(d)); DoD requests per PGI 228.305(d); in the Army the recommendation is delegated from ASA(ALT) to the HCA, no lower than SCO (AFARS 5128.305(d); Appendix GG Rev. 30).

DoL Waiver 2026-02 (ROK, 26 Mar 2026 to 25 Mar 2031) waives DBA for employees covered under Korea's compulsory workers' compensation laws when the employer complies; it excludes U.S. citizens, U.S. lawful residents and anyone hired in the U.S.

Waived employees still need War Hazards Compensation Act-equivalent protection; third-country nationals fall within the waiver only if covered by Korean compulsory law with benefits that continue after repatriation.
Clauses: 52.228-3 when DBA applies, 52.228-4 when DoL has waived it (28.309); a mixed workforce likely needs both; confirm locally.

question: You administer a $45 million services contract that ends in March 2027. What does RFO FAR subpart 42.11 require for past performance evaluations, who is the Army assessing official, and how are contractor disagreements and integrity reports handled?
answer:
When. Evaluations are due at least annually and at completion, including overseas work (RFO FAR 42.1102(a)). DoD uses its own thresholds instead of the FAR's SAT tiers: services and IT over $1 million, systems and operations support over $5 million, ship repair over $500,000 (DFARS 242.1102-70(b); 215.104-70(g)). Construction is evaluated at $900,000 and A-E at $45,000, plus any default termination (42.1102(e)-(f)). All go into CPARS (42.1101(b)).

Who assesses in the Army (AFARS 5142.1103-90): the contracting officer for services, or the program manager for services supporting a program office; the program manager for systems; the contracting officer for operations support, IT, construction, A-E and all others. Each job order contract order of $700,000 or more gets an assessment.

Content. A plain description of the contract and five-level ratings with fact-based narratives for technical quality, cost control (not for firm-fixed-price), schedule, management, small business subcontracting including unjustified reduced or late payments, and other areas (42.1103(b)). A marginal or unsatisfactory rating should cite the letter or report that notified the contractor (Table 42-1).

Contractor rights. Up to 14 calendar days to comment; the evaluation reaches source selection officials within 14 days of notification; disagreements are reviewed above the contracting officer; the final goes to the contractor (42.1103(d)-(e)).

Shelf life. Source selections use CPARS data within 3 years of completion, 6 for construction and A-E (42.1103(f)); no record is rated neutral (15.202(c)(1)).

Integrity. Within 3 calendar days FAPIIS must show defective pricing determinations, default terminations and conversions, substantiated trafficking violations, and a history of unjustified reduced or late payments to small business subcontractors; that information is public (42.1103(g)).

Late or inflated evaluations hurt the next source selection.

Cite: RFO FAR 42.1101, 42.1102, 42.1103, 15.202(c); DFARS 242.1102-70 (Class Deviation 2026-O0050), 215.104-70(g) (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev. 1); AFARS 5142.1103-90.
key_points: Evaluations at least annually and at completion, including overseas work; DoD thresholds replace the FAR's SAT tiers: services and IT over $1M, systems and operations support over $5M, ship repair over $500K (DFARS 242.1102-70(b); 215.104-70(g)); construction at $900K or more and A-E at $45K or more (RFO FAR 42.1102(e)-(f)).
Army assessing official: KO for services (PM for services supporting a program office), PM for systems, KO for operations support, IT, construction, A-E and all others (AFARS 5142.1103-90(a)).
The contractor has up to 14 calendar days to comment; disagreements are reviewed above the KO (42.1103(d)-(e)).
Source selections use CPARS data within 3 years of completion (6 for construction and A-E) (42.1103(f)); no record is neutral (15.202(c)(1)).
FAPIIS entries within 3 calendar days for defective pricing determinations, default terminations and other integrity events (42.1103(g)).
